summary: How one bipotential gonad and two pairs of ducts become male or female organs, and how the placenta and breast form. Exam questions give a karyotype, a hormone defect, or a birth defect and ask you to predict the anatomy that results.

points: Until about week 7 the gonad is bipotential (indifferent) and both duct pairs are present.
SRY on the short arm of the Y chromosome codes for testis-determining factor, which turns supporting cells into Sertoli cells and the gonad into a testis.
Without SRY the gonad becomes an ovary by default.
46,XY with an SRY deletion: no testis forms, the gonads become streaks, and the person has a uterus, tubes, and female external genitalia (Swyer syndrome).
46,XX with SRY translocated onto an X: testes form and the phenotype is male, but the testes are small and sperm are not made because other Y genes for spermatogenesis are missing.
notes.why: SRY is a transcription factor that switches on SOX9 in the supporting cells of the genital ridge, turning them into Sertoli cells; once Sertoli cells exist they organize testis cords and pull the rest of the gonad into testis development. When this switch is absent, as in a 46,XY embryo with an SRY deletion, the gonads become streaks that make neither AMH nor testosterone, so the ducts and external genitalia follow the female path. A translocated SRY flips the switch in a 46,XX gonad, yet spermatogenesis still fails because the azoospermia factor (AZF) genes on the long arm of the Y chromosome are missing.

points: Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), which makes the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts regress.
Leydig cells make testosterone, first driven by placental hCG and later by fetal LH.
Testosterone keeps the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts, which form the epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle, and ejaculatory duct.
5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which builds the penis, scrotum, and prostate.
With no AMH and no testosterone (female), the Mullerian ducts persist and the Wolffian ducts regress, leaving at most a Gartner duct cyst.
notes.why: Male duct and genital development needs three separate signals, so each one can fail on its own. AMH acts locally on the paramesonephric ducts, testosterone acts locally on the mesonephric ducts, and the external genitalia and prostate need DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more tightly than testosterone. This predicts the classic patterns: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency gives normal internal male ducts with ambiguous external genitalia, while complete androgen insensitivity gives testes and absent Mullerian structures (AMH still works) with female external genitalia and a blind vaginal pouch.

points: The unfused cranial parts of the paramesonephric ducts become the uterine tubes.
The caudal parts fuse in the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus (sinovaginal bulbs).
After fusion the wall between the two ducts must be resorbed to leave one cavity.
No fusion gives uterus didelphys (two uteri, two cervices, often a double vagina); partial fusion gives a bicornuate uterus; failed septum resorption gives a septate uterus.
Ovaries come from the gonadal ridge, so ovarian function is normal in Mullerian defects; renal anomalies often travel with them.
notes.why: The uterus forms in three steps: the two paramesonephric ducts grow down, fuse in the midline, and then resorb the septum between them. The defect tells you which step failed: no fusion gives didelphys, incomplete fusion of the upper part gives a bicornuate uterus with an indented fundus, and failed resorption gives a septate uterus with a normal outer contour. The paramesonephric ducts depend on the nearby mesonephric ducts, which also give rise to the ureteric bud, so renal agenesis or ectopy often accompanies these defects, while the ovaries arise separately from the gonadal ridge and keep normal function.

points: Genital tubercle: glans penis or glans clitoris.
Urogenital folds: ventral shaft of the penis around the spongy (penile) urethra, or labia minora.
Labioscrotal swellings: scrotum or labia majora.
Hypospadias (ventral urethral opening) means the urogenital folds did not fuse; epispadias (dorsal opening) comes from a misplaced genital tubercle and is linked to bladder exstrophy.
notes.why: The same three primordia are present in both sexes, and DHT acting through the androgen receptor decides whether they enlarge and fuse (male) or stay separate (female). In the male the urogenital folds fuse along the ventral midline over the urethral groove to close the spongy urethra, so incomplete fusion leaves the opening on the ventral side (hypospadias). Epispadias comes from a different error, an abnormal position of the genital tubercle relative to the cloacal membrane, which explains its link to bladder exstrophy.

points: The testis starts high on the posterior abdominal wall, so its artery comes off the aorta and its lymph drains to para-aortic nodes.
The gubernaculum anchors the testis and guides it through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, usually by birth.
A pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, goes ahead of the testis and normally closes, leaving only the tunica vaginalis around the testis.
A wide patent processus vaginalis lets bowel enter the cord: indirect inguinal hernia through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
A narrow patent processus lets only peritoneal fluid through: communicating hydrocele that changes size and transilluminates.
In the female the gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus.
notes.why: The testis develops in the lumbar region and keeps the blood supply and lymph drainage it acquired there, which is why testicular cancer spreads first to para-aortic nodes. The gubernaculum guides descent in a transabdominal phase and an androgen-dependent inguinoscrotal phase. The processus vaginalis must close after descent, and the width of any channel left open decides whether bowel (indirect hernia) or only fluid (communicating hydrocele) can follow it; both enter through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

points: Fetal part: chorion frondosum (villous chorion). Maternal part: decidua basalis.
Villi have an inner cytotrophoblast layer and an outer syncytiotrophoblast layer, which makes hCG and faces maternal blood.
The umbilical cord holds two umbilical arteries (deoxygenated blood to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (oxygenated blood to the fetus) in Wharton jelly.
A single umbilical artery is linked to congenital anomalies, especially renal and cardiac.
notes.why: The placenta forms where the villous chorion meets the decidua basalis, so maternal and fetal blood exchange across the villus wall without mixing. The syncytiotrophoblast, the outer layer bathed in maternal blood, is a multinucleated layer formed by fusion of cytotrophoblast cells, and it does the hormone work (hCG, hPL, progesterone, estrogen). Umbilical vessels are named for direction relative to the fetal heart: the arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus and the vein brings oxygenated blood back. A single umbilical artery is a marker that should prompt a search for renal and cardiac anomalies.

points: The breast starts as an ectodermal thickening, the mammary ridge (milk line), running from the axilla to the groin on each side.
Only the pectoral part of the ridge normally survives and sends cords into the mesenchyme that become the lactiferous ducts.
Parts of the ridge that fail to regress give supernumerary nipples (polythelia) or extra breast tissue (polymastia) anywhere along the line, most often in the axilla or on the lower chest or abdomen.
notes.why: The mammary ridge is a band of surface ectoderm, so the breast is a modified sweat gland that grows down into the underlying mesenchyme. Normally the ridge regresses everywhere except over the pectoral region, where epithelial buds branch into about 15 to 20 lactiferous ducts. Any segment that persists can form a nipple or glandular tissue, which is why accessory tissue appears along the axilla to groin line and can respond to hormones and develop the same diseases as the breast.

tricks.label: SEED
tricks.text: Wolffian duct derivatives: Seminal vesicles, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Ductus deferens.

tricks.label: Outside or inside
tricks.text: Look at the outer contour of the uterus. A notch on the outside means a fusion problem (bicornuate); a smooth outside with a wall inside means a resorption problem (septate).

tricks.label: Who makes what
tricks.text: Sertoli makes AMH, Leydig makes testosterone, 5-alpha-reductase in genital tissue makes DHT. Lose AMH and a uterus stays; lose testosterone action and the Wolffian ducts fade; lose DHT and the outside looks female.

highYield: SRY absent or deleted means ovary or streak gonad; SRY present, even on an X, means testis.
Androgen insensitivity (46,XY): AMH still works, so there is no uterus and a short blind vagina, yet external genitalia are female and testes sit in the abdomen, inguinal canal, or labia.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency (46,XY): normal Wolffian structures, ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth, and virilization at puberty.
Septate uterus carries the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss among the fusion defects.
Indirect inguinal hernia and communicating hydrocele are the same defect, a patent processus vaginalis, differing only in its width.
Two arteries and one vein in the cord; a single umbilical artery prompts a search for renal and heart anomalies.
Extra nipples lie along the milk line from axilla to groin.
pitfalls: Hypospadias is ventral and from unfused urogenital folds; epispadias is dorsal and from a misplaced genital tubercle.
Testosterone builds the internal male ducts; DHT builds the external genitalia and prostate.
The upper vagina is Mullerian; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus.
A communicating hydrocele changes size during the day; a noncommunicating hydrocele has a closed processus and a fixed size.

summary: The cells and tissues of the testis, ovary, female tract, breast, and prostate. Exam questions show a cell or a zone and ask what it makes or which disease starts there.

points: Sertoli cells sit inside the seminiferous tubules and stretch from the basement membrane to the lumen.
Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, which shields developing haploid germ cells from the immune system.
Sertoli cells respond to FSH and make androgen-binding protein (keeps testosterone high in the tubule), inhibin B (feeds back to lower FSH), and AMH in the fetus.
Leydig cells sit in the interstitium between tubules near capillaries; they respond to LH and make testosterone.
Leydig cells look like pink polygonal cells with lipid droplets and sometimes Reinke crystals.
Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis are damaged by heat; Leydig cells are not, so testosterone stays normal in an undescended testis.
notes.why: Spermatogenesis needs two inputs: FSH acting on Sertoli cells and a very high local testosterone level from Leydig cells under LH, held in the tubule by androgen-binding protein. Sertoli tight junctions divide the epithelium into a basal compartment, where spermatogonia sit, and an adluminal compartment, where meiotic and haploid cells carry new antigens the immune system never learned as self. Feedback is split the same way: inhibin B from Sertoli cells lowers FSH, while testosterone lowers LH and GnRH.

points: Seminiferous tubules, straight tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis (head, body, tail).
Ductus deferens, then the ejaculatory duct after it joins the seminal vesicle duct.
Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra, spongy (penile) urethra.
The epididymis is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia; sperm gain motility and are stored there.
notes.why: The path runs from the site of production to sites of maturation, storage, and propulsion. Efferent ductules carry sperm from the rete testis to the head of the epididymis, where sperm spend days gaining forward motility and the ability to fertilize; the stereocilia are long microvilli that absorb fluid and concentrate the sperm. At emission, smooth muscle in the ductus deferens propels sperm into the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra, so a blockage anywhere along this path causes azoospermia with normal testosterone.

points: Uterine tube: simple columnar with ciliated cells and secretory (peg) cells; cilia move the egg toward the uterus.
Endometrium: simple columnar with tubular glands; the functional layer sheds and the basal layer regrows it.
Endocervix: simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium.
Ectocervix and vagina: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The transformation zone is the area of squamous metaplasia at the squamocolumnar junction; HPV infection and cervical dysplasia arise here, so the Pap smear samples it.
notes.why: Each epithelium fits its job: ciliated columnar cells move the oocyte along the tube, glandular columnar cells secrete mucus in the endocervix, and stratified squamous cells resist friction in the vagina and ectocervix. Where columnar epithelium of the endocervix is exposed to acidic vaginal pH, reserve cells undergo squamous metaplasia, and these immature metaplastic cells are the cells high-risk HPV infects most readily. That is why dysplasia and carcinoma begin in the transformation zone and why an adequate Pap sample must include it.

points: Every follicle holds a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I until the LH surge.
Granulosa cells surround the oocyte; theca cells form outside the basement membrane once the follicle grows.
Theca interna makes androgens under LH, and granulosa cells convert them to estradiol with aromatase under FSH.
After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, made of large granulosa lutein cells and smaller theca lutein cells that secrete progesterone and estrogen.
notes.why: Follicle stages track the granulosa layer: one flat layer (primordial), a cuboidal layer that becomes several layers (primary), fluid-filled spaces that merge into an antrum (secondary), and a large antrum with the oocyte on the cumulus oophorus (mature, Graafian). Estradiol synthesis needs both cell types (the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model): theca cells have LH receptors and make androgens but lack aromatase, while granulosa cells have aromatase induced by FSH and convert the androgen that diffuses in. After ovulation LH luteinizes both cell types, and the corpus luteum shifts to mainly progesterone output.

points: The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is a terminal duct with its cluster of small ductules (acini).
Each duct and acinus has two cell layers: inner luminal epithelial cells and outer myoepithelial cells on a basement membrane.
Most breast carcinomas, both ductal and lobular, arise in the TDLU.
Fibroadenoma arises from the specialized stroma of the TDLU and contains both stroma and ducts.
Loss of the myoepithelial layer around tumor nests marks invasive carcinoma.
notes.why: The two-layer structure is the key to reading breast pathology. Benign lesions and carcinoma in situ keep the myoepithelial layer and basement membrane around the epithelium, while invasive carcinoma has broken through them into the stroma, so stains for myoepithelial markers help separate the two. The TDLU is the hormonally responsive part of the duct system, which is why both carcinoma and the stromal and epithelial fibroadenoma arise there.

points: Peripheral zone: posterior and lateral, largest share of glandular tissue, felt on digital rectal exam; most carcinomas arise here.
Transition zone: surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra; benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises here and compresses the urethra.
Central zone: surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is seldom diseased.
Prostate glands have luminal secretory cells over basal cells; carcinoma glands lack the basal cell layer.
notes.why: The zones differ in position, and position decides symptoms. The transition zone surrounds the urethra, so nodular hyperplasia there narrows the lumen and causes hesitancy, weak stream, and retention, often before the gland feels very large. The peripheral zone lies against the rectum and away from the urethra, so carcinoma there is often found as a hard nodule on digital rectal exam and gives urinary symptoms only late. Carcinoma glands lose the basal cell layer, a feature pathologists use to separate cancer from benign glands.

tricks.label: SEVEN UP
tricks.text: Sperm pathway: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

tricks.label: Sertoli supports, Leydig lives on LH
tricks.text: Sertoli cells Support sperm and answer to FSH; Leydig cells answer to LH and make testosterone.

tricks.label: Peripheral is palpable
tricks.text: Cancer starts in the peripheral zone, which lies against the rectum, so a hard nodule is felt on rectal exam. BPH grows in the middle around the urethra, so it blocks urine flow early.

highYield: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells selectively lowers FSH; testosterone lowers LH.
The blood-testis barrier explains antisperm antibodies after trauma, vasectomy, or mumps orchitis.
Cryptorchidism lowers sperm count but leaves testosterone normal because heat harms Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells.
The Pap smear and HPV testing target the transformation zone.
Ciliary damage in the uterine tube (as after salpingitis) slows the egg and raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
BPH arises in the transition zone and usually spares the peripheral zone, so it does not predispose to prostate cancer.
pitfalls: Theca interna makes androgens under LH; granulosa cells aromatize them to estradiol under FSH.
Endocervix is columnar and ectocervix is squamous; the vagina is squamous throughout and has no glands.
Fibroadenoma comes from TDLU stroma; carcinoma comes from TDLU epithelium.
The oocyte in a Graafian follicle is still primary until the LH surge triggers completion of meiosis I.

summary: How sperm and eggs are made, how they meet, and what happens from the zygote through week 8. Exam questions test meiotic arrest points, the steps of fertilization, where implantation goes wrong, and when the embryo is most vulnerable.

points: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty and runs continuously in the seminiferous tubules; one cycle takes about 64 to 74 days.
Each primary spermatocyte gives four functional spermatids after two meiotic divisions.
Oogonia multiply only before birth; those that survive become primary oocytes that arrest in prophase I and stay arrested until the LH surge before ovulation.
At the LH surge the oocyte finishes meiosis I, sheds the first polar body, and arrests again in metaphase II.
Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters, giving the ovum and the second polar body.
Each primary oocyte yields one functional ovum; the polar bodies degenerate.
The years-long arrest in prophase I is linked to more nondisjunction with older maternal age.
notes.why: Spermatogonia are a self-renewing stem cell pool, so a man makes sperm continuously from puberty, whereas the female germ cell pool is fixed before birth and only declines. Male meiosis divides cytoplasm equally into four spermatids, while oocyte divisions are unequal, sending almost all cytoplasm to one cell and discarding the extra chromosomes in polar bodies. The first oocyte arrest is released by the LH surge and the second by sperm entry. A primary oocyte can stay in prophase I for decades, and the cohesion holding homologous chromosomes together weakens over that time, which is one explanation for the rise in nondisjunction and trisomy with maternal age.

points: Spermiogenesis turns a round spermatid into a sperm without any cell division.
The Golgi apparatus forms the acrosome, a cap of enzymes over the nucleus.
A centriole forms the flagellum; mitochondria pack into the midpiece to power it.
The nucleus condenses and extra cytoplasm is shed as a residual body that Sertoli cells engulf.
Capacitation happens in the female tract over several hours: proteins and cholesterol are stripped from the sperm membrane and motility becomes hyperactive.
Only a capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction after binding the zona pellucida, releasing enzymes that digest a path through it.
notes.why: Spermiogenesis remodels a round haploid cell into a streamlined swimming cell with no further division. The Golgi packs hydrolytic enzymes into the acrosome for crossing the zona pellucida, the centriole builds the axoneme of the flagellum, and midpiece mitochondria supply ATP for dynein-driven beating, which is why a dynein arm defect (primary ciliary dyskinesia) causes immotile sperm and infertility. Freshly ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize because cholesterol and coating glycoproteins stabilize the membrane; removing them in the female tract (capacitation) destabilizes the membrane so that zona binding can trigger acrosomal exocytosis.

points: Fertilization usually happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube within about 24 hours of ovulation.
When the sperm and oocyte membranes fuse, calcium rises in the oocyte and cortical granules release enzymes that change the zona pellucida (cortical reaction), blocking other sperm.
The oocyte then completes meiosis II; male and female pronuclei join to form a diploid zygote.
The sperm sets genetic sex by carrying an X or a Y chromosome.
notes.why: Sperm and oocyte fusion triggers a wave of calcium release from the oocyte endoplasmic reticulum, and this one signal does two jobs. It drives exocytosis of cortical granules, whose enzymes modify the zona pellucida so it no longer binds or admits sperm (block to polyspermy), and it releases the metaphase II arrest so the oocyte completes meiosis II and extrudes the second polar body. Fertilization therefore restores diploidy and sets genetic sex, because the oocyte always contributes an X while the sperm contributes an X or a Y.

points: The zygote cleaves as it moves down the tube, reaching the uterus as a morula around day 3 to 4.
The blastocyst has an inner cell mass (becomes the embryo) and an outer trophoblast (becomes placenta), and it hatches from the zona pellucida before implanting.
Implantation begins about day 6 in the secretory-phase endometrium, usually on the posterior wall of the uterine body.
Syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone so the endometrium is not shed.
hCG is detectable in maternal blood about 1 week after fertilization.
notes.why: Cleavage divisions add cells without growth, so the conceptus stays small enough to travel down the tube inside the zona pellucida, which also prevents it from attaching too early. Fluid then collects to form the blastocyst, separating trophoblast from inner cell mass; after hatching, the trophoblast attaches to the receptive secretory endometrium prepared by progesterone. Syncytiotrophoblast hCG acts on the LH receptor of the corpus luteum, keeping progesterone high so the endometrium (now decidua) is not shed and menses does not occur.

points: Tubal ectopic pregnancy: most often in the ampulla; prior salpingitis (PID from chlamydia or gonorrhea) is a main risk because scarring and cilia loss slow the embryo.
Other ectopic risks: prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, and pregnancy with an IUD in place.
Ectopic presentation: missed period, pelvic pain, and spotting with a lower hCG than expected; rupture causes hemorrhage that pools in the rectouterine pouch.
Placenta previa: implantation in the lower uterine segment so the placenta covers or reaches the internal cervical os, causing painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy.
Prior cesarean scar, multiparity, and older maternal age raise previa risk.
notes.why: The blastocyst implants wherever it is when it is ready to attach, so anything that slows transport through the tube, such as scarring and loss of cilia after salpingitis, leaves it to implant in the tube wall. The tube cannot form a proper decidua or expand, so the trophoblast erodes into vessels and the tube can rupture, and poor trophoblast growth explains the lower than expected hCG. In placenta previa the placenta lies over the lower uterine segment, which thins and stretches in the third trimester; this shears placental attachments and causes painless bleeding, and a digital cervical exam can provoke heavy hemorrhage.

points: Week 2: bilaminar disc of epiblast and hypoblast, with the amniotic cavity above and the yolk sac below.
Week 3: gastrulation; epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), and the notochord forms.
Weeks 3 to 8 (embryonic period) are when organs form, so teratogens cause major structural defects then.
Before week 3 an exposure is all or none: the embryo dies or recovers fully.
notes.why: Week 2 is often called the week of twos: two layers of the disc (epiblast and hypoblast), two cavities, and two trophoblast layers. In week 3 epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak, replacing the hypoblast to form endoderm and filling the middle layer as mesoderm, while the remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm, so all three germ layers come from epiblast. Before gastrulation the cells are still undifferentiated and can replace lost neighbors, which explains the all-or-none effect; once organ primordia are laid down in weeks 3 to 8, injury removes a structure that cannot be rebuilt, causing major malformations.

flows.title: Oogenesis from fetus to fertilization
steps: Oogonia multiply by mitosis in the fetal ovary
Primary oocytes enter meiosis I and arrest in prophase I before birth
LH surge: meiosis I completes and the first polar body forms
Secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and is ovulated
Sperm entry: meiosis II completes and the second polar body forms
Female and male pronuclei join to form a diploid zygote

flows.title: Fertilization
steps: Capacitation in the female tract removes cholesterol and surface glycoproteins
Hyperactive sperm passes the corona radiata and binds the zona pellucida
Zona binding triggers the acrosome reaction; enzymes digest a path
Sperm and oocyte membranes fuse, and oocyte calcium rises
Cortical granules release enzymes that alter the zona, blocking polyspermy
Oocyte completes meiosis II, and the pronuclei form the zygote

flows.title: Zygote to implantation

All three germ layers come from the epiblast.

summary: Where the reproductive organs sit and what holds them in place: pelvic ligaments and pouches, the pelvic floor, the scrotum and spermatic cord, the breast, the penis, and the perineum. Exam questions link a structure to its contents, its support, or what happens when it tears or weakens.

points: The broad ligament is a double fold of peritoneum draped from the sides of the uterus to the lateral pelvic walls.
Mesometrium: the largest part, beside the uterus. Mesosalpinx: around the uterine tube. Mesovarium: attaches the ovary to the back of the broad ligament.
The vesicouterine pouch lies between bladder and uterus; the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) lies between uterus and rectum.
The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in a standing woman, so blood or pus collects there; it can be reached through the posterior vaginal fornix.
In the male the lowest recess is the rectovesical pouch.
notes.why: The broad ligament is peritoneum draped over the uterus, tubes, and ovaries, and each subdivision is named for the organ it holds: metra (uterus), salpinx (tube), ovarium (ovary). In front of and behind the uterus the peritoneum dips into recesses, and gravity carries free fluid to the most dependent one, the rectouterine pouch, when the woman stands. Only the thin posterior vaginal fornix separates this pouch from the vagina, so fluid there can be seen on ultrasound or sampled (culdocentesis) to look for blood after a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

points: Suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament: ovary to lateral pelvic wall; carries the ovarian artery and vein.
Ovarian ligament: ovary to the side of the uterus; no major vessels.
Round ligament: uterine horn through the deep ring and inguinal canal to the labium majus.
Cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament: cervix to lateral pelvic wall; carries the uterine artery and vein.
Uterosacral ligaments: cervix back to the sacrum; they hold the cervix posteriorly.
notes.why: The ligaments make sense once you know which vessels each one carries. The ovary is supplied from above by the ovarian vessels, which reach it from the posterior abdominal wall through the suspensory ligament, while the uterus is supplied from the side by the uterine vessels running in the base of the broad ligament (cardinal ligament). The ovarian and round ligaments are the two remnants of the female gubernaculum, which is why the round ligament follows the same inguinal path as the descending testis and ends in the labium majus, the female counterpart of the scrotum.

points: The levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) forms most of the pelvic floor and holds up the pelvic organs.
The perineal body is a fibromuscular knot between the vagina and anus where perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter attach.
The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments suspend the cervix and upper vagina from above.
Vaginal childbirth, aging and low estrogen after menopause, obesity, and chronic cough or straining weaken these supports.
Weak support lets organs drop: uterine prolapse (uterus into the vagina), cystocele (bladder into the anterior wall), rectocele (rectum into the posterior wall).
notes.why: Pelvic organs are held up by two systems working together: active support from the constant tone of the levator ani, which keeps the urogenital hiatus narrow, and passive suspension of the cervix and upper vagina by the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments. Vaginal delivery can stretch or tear the levator ani and its nerve supply, and estrogen loss after menopause weakens the collagen in pelvic connective tissue. When the muscle fails, the ligaments carry the whole load and gradually stretch, so the organ behind the weakened wall bulges into the vaginal canal.

points: Scrotal layers from outside in: skin, dartos fascia and muscle, external spermatic fascia, cremaster muscle and fascia, internal spermatic fascia, tunica vaginalis.
The spermatic fasciae come from the abdominal wall layers the testis passed through: external oblique, internal oblique, and transversalis fascia.
Cord contents: ductus deferens, testicular artery, artery to the ductus, cremasteric artery, pampiniform venous plexus, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, autonomic nerves, and lymphatics.
The pampiniform plexus cools arterial blood going to the testis; its dilation is a varicocele.
notes.why: As the testis descended through the inguinal canal it pushed out a sleeve of each abdominal wall layer, so each scrotal layer matches a layer of the anterior abdominal wall. External spermatic fascia comes from the external oblique aponeurosis, the cremaster from the internal oblique, internal spermatic fascia from the transversalis fascia, and the tunica vaginalis from the processus vaginalis of peritoneum. The pampiniform plexus wraps the testicular artery and cools incoming blood by countercurrent heat exchange, keeping the testis about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) below core temperature; a varicocele weakens this exchange.

points: The breast lies on the pectoralis major and serratus anterior from about rib 2 to rib 6, and from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line.
A loose retromammary space lets the breast slide over the pectoral fascia.
The axillary tail extends toward the axilla; the upper outer quadrant holds the most glandular tissue and the most cancers.
Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments run from the dermis to the deep fascia; carcinoma that pulls on them causes skin dimpling.
notes.why: The breast sits in the superficial fascia and is separated from the pectoral fascia by the retromammary space, so a normal breast moves freely over the chest wall. Suspensory ligaments tether the dermis to the deep fascia; when carcinoma infiltrates and shortens them, the overlying skin is pulled inward, causing dimpling, and fixation of a mass to the pectoral muscle means invasion through the retromammary space. Blocked dermal lymphatics cause a different sign, peau d'orange, from skin edema pitted at the hair follicles. The upper outer quadrant holds the most glandular tissue, so it also has the most cancers.

points: Two corpora cavernosa lie dorsally; one corpus spongiosum lies ventrally around the urethra and expands into the glans.
Each corpus is wrapped in a tough tunica albuginea, thickest around the corpora cavernosa.
Penile fracture is a tear of the tunica albuginea of a corpus cavernosum when the erect penis is forcefully bent: a pop, sudden loss of erection, swelling, and bruising.
The perineum is diamond-shaped: pubic symphysis in front, ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities at the sides, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx behind.
A line between the ischial tuberosities splits it into the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle.
The prostate lies below the bladder and in front of the rectum, so its posterior surface is felt through the anterior rectal wall on digital rectal exam.
notes.why: The erectile bodies are built for rigidity: the thick tunica albuginea around the corpora cavernosa limits expansion, which lets pressure inside them rise during erection. When an erect penis is forcefully bent, this stretched and thinned tunica can tear and release blood into the shaft, while the corpus spongiosum has a thinner tunica and stays softer so the urethra remains open. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into a urogenital triangle in front, holding the external genitalia and urethra, and an anal triangle behind. The prostate sits just in front of the rectum, so its posterior surface is felt on rectal exam.

tricks.text: As the testis passed through the abdominal wall, each layer gave it a covering in the same order: external oblique outside, internal oblique in the middle, transversalis fascia inside, peritoneum innermost.

The suspensory ligament of the ovary carries the ovarian vessels; the cardinal ligament carries the uterine vessels.
The round ligament travels through the inguinal canal, filling the place the spermatic cord takes in the male.

Penile fracture tears the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum.
Cystocele bulges from the anterior vaginal wall; rectocele bulges from the posterior wall.
The prostate lies directly in front of the rectum, so the peripheral zone is reachable by digital rectal exam.
pitfalls: The ovarian ligament connects ovary to uterus and carries no major vessels; the suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels.
Cremaster comes from the internal oblique; the external spermatic fascia comes from the external oblique.
Dimpling comes from Cooper ligament traction; peau d'orange comes from blocked dermal lymphatics.
The corpus spongiosum surrounds the urethra; the corpora cavernosa do not.

summary: The arteries, veins, lymph nodes, and nerves of the reproductive organs and breast. Exam questions ask why a varicocele is left-sided, which structure is injured in a pelvic operation, where a tumor spreads first, and which nerve controls each step of the male sexual response.

points: Both gonadal arteries come off the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries, because the gonads started high on the posterior wall.
The right gonadal vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava at an angle.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle after a longer course.
The longer column of blood and right-angle entry raise pressure on the left, so varicocele is far more common on the left.
A varicocele feels like a bag of worms, grows with standing or straining, and can lower fertility by warming the testis.
A new varicocele on the right, or one that does not empty when lying down, suggests a mass blocking venous drainage.
notes.why: The gonads develop in the upper lumbar region and keep their vessels as they descend, so the gonadal arteries still arise from the aorta near the renal arteries. Venous return is asymmetric: the right vein joins the inferior vena cava at an oblique angle, while the left vein is longer and drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. Higher hydrostatic pressure and incompetent valves on the left dilate the pampiniform plexus, while a right-sided or nonreducing varicocele suggests a mass, such as a renal tumor, blocking outflow.

points: The uterine artery comes from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
It runs medially in the base of the broad ligament (cardinal ligament) toward the cervix, then climbs up the side of the uterus.
About 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery.
Clamping the uterine vessels during hysterectomy can catch or cut the ureter, causing hydronephrosis or a urine leak.
The uterine artery joins with the ovarian artery near the uterine horn.
notes.why: The ureter descends along the lateral pelvic wall and then turns medially toward the bladder, passing under the uterine artery in the base of the broad ligament about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"). Here the two structures are close enough that a clamp placed on the uterine vessels can take the ureter as well. Ligation obstructs urine flow from that kidney, causing hydronephrosis and flank pain, while a cut or devascularized ureter leaks urine into the pelvis or forms a fistula to the vagina, so surgeons identify the ureter before ligating the uterine vessels.

points: Testis and ovary drain to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, following the gonadal vessels back to their origin.
Uterine body, cervix, and upper vagina drain to internal and external iliac nodes.
Scrotum, vulva, and the lower vagina below the hymen drain to superficial inguinal nodes.
A testicular tumor spreads first to para-aortic nodes; a scrotal skin cancer spreads first to inguinal nodes.
notes.why: Lymph usually follows the arteries that supply an organ back toward their origin, and this rule predicts most first nodal sites. The gonads draw their arteries from the aorta, so their lymph runs to para-aortic nodes, while the uterus and cervix are supplied from the internal iliac system and drain to iliac nodes. Skin and surface structures below the umbilicus, including the scrotum, vulva, and distal vagina, drain to superficial inguinal nodes, so an enlarged inguinal node points to a skin or vulvar source and away from the testis.

notes.h: Nerves of the male sexual response
points: Erection: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) through the cavernous nerves.
Emission: sympathetic hypogastric nerves move semen into the prostatic urethra and close the internal urethral sphincter.
Ejaculation: the somatic pudendal nerve drives rhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle.
Cavernous nerve injury in pelvic surgery causes erectile dysfunction; loss of sympathetic tone at the bladder neck causes retrograde ejaculation.
notes.why: The three phases are run by three divisions of the nervous system. Parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 travel in the cavernous nerves and release nitric oxide to dilate penile arteries (erection). Sympathetic fibers from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar cord, through the hypogastric nerves, contract the smooth muscle of the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate to load semen into the urethra and close the bladder neck so semen goes forward (emission). The somatic pudendal nerve then drives the striated bulbospongiosus muscle to expel semen (ejaculation).

points: Roots S2 to S4. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis.
It hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen.
It runs in the pudendal canal to the perineum and gives the inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris.
The ischial spine is the landmark for a pudendal nerve block, felt through the vaginal wall during labor.
Injury from childbirth or prolonged cycling causes perineal numbness and can weaken the external urethral and anal sphincters.
notes.why: The pudendal nerve takes an indirect route: it leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, crosses behind the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine, and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the perineum below the pelvic floor. Because it crosses the ischial spine, anesthetic placed there through the vaginal wall blocks sensation to most of the perineum during the second stage of labor. The nerve carries both sensory fibers from perineal skin and motor fibers to the external anal and urethral sphincters, so stretch or compression injury causes numbness together with fecal or urinary incontinence.

points: Arteries: perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery (medial breast), lateral thoracic artery, and pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery, with help from intercostal arteries.
Most lymph (about three quarters) drains to axillary nodes, so the axilla is the first site checked for spread.
Medial quadrants also drain to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.
Axillary node surgery can cause arm lymphedema and can injure the long thoracic nerve, giving a winged scapula.
notes.why: Breast arteries come from the vessels next to it: the internal thoracic medially, the lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial branches of the axillary artery laterally, and the intercostal arteries. Lymph follows a similar pattern, with lateral and central drainage running to axillary nodes and medial lymph passing through the chest wall to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels. This is why sentinel node biopsy targets the axilla, and why a medial tumor can spread to internal thoracic nodes that axillary surgery does not reach. Removing axillary nodes blocks lymph return from the arm, causing lymphedema, and the long thoracic nerve on the serratus anterior lies in the dissection field.

pitfalls: The scrotum and testis drain to different nodes: inguinal for the scrotum, para-aortic for the testis.

summary: How the menstrual cycle, erection, pregnancy, lactation, and labor work. Exam questions ask you to predict a hormone level, a lab value in pregnancy, or the next step in a feedback loop.

points: Follicular phase: FSH grows a dominant follicle whose estradiol drives the proliferative phase of the endometrium.
High sustained estradiol switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge; ovulation follows about 36 hours after the surge begins.

Luteal phase: the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which turns the endometrium secretory (coiled glands, glycogen, edematous stroma) and raises basal body temperature about 0.3 to 0.5 °C (0.5 to 0.9 °F).
Without hCG the corpus luteum lasts about 14 days, then regresses; falling progesterone causes spiral artery spasm and shedding of the functional layer (menses).
The luteal phase is fixed near 14 days, so differences in cycle length come from the follicular phase.
Ovulation therefore happens about 14 days before the next period, whatever the cycle length.
notes.why: The cycle turns on the switch of estradiol from negative to positive feedback. Early follicular estradiol and inhibin lower FSH, so only the follicle with the most FSH receptors and aromatase survives; once that follicle keeps estradiol high and sustained, the pituitary responds with an LH surge that ruptures the follicle and luteinizes it. The corpus luteum has a built-in lifespan of about 14 days unless hCG rescues it, which fixes the luteal phase, so variation in cycle length comes from how long the follicle takes to mature. Progesterone acts on the hypothalamic temperature set point, explaining the temperature rise after ovulation.

points: Parasympathetic nerves and endothelium release nitric oxide (NO).
NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP and lowering calcium in cavernosal smooth muscle, which relaxes.
Arterial inflow fills the sinusoids, which swell and press the small veins against the tunica albuginea, trapping blood.
Phosphodiesterase 5 breaks down cGMP to end the erection; PDE5 inhibitors prolong it.
notes.why: Erection is a blood flow event controlled by smooth muscle tone. Nitric oxide from parasympathetic nerve endings and endothelium diffuses into cavernosal smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase; cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic calcium and relaxes the muscle of the arterioles and sinusoids. Filling sinusoids compress the small venules against the rigid tunica albuginea (veno-occlusion), so outflow falls as inflow rises. PDE5 inhibitors keep cGMP high but depend on NO release, so they work poorly after cavernous nerve injury, and combining them with nitrates causes dangerous hypotension.

points: hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast acts on the LH receptor to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone.
By about weeks 7 to 10 the placenta makes enough progesterone itself (luteal-placental shift), near the end of the first trimester.
The placenta lacks the enzyme (17-alpha-hydroxylase) to make androgens, so it needs fetal adrenal DHEA-S to make estrogen.
Fetal adrenal DHEA-S is 16-hydroxylated in the fetal liver, then turned into estriol by the placenta; low estriol can mean a problem in the fetal adrenal, liver, or placenta.
Human placental lactogen (hPL) rises with placental mass, causes maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, and spares glucose for the fetus.
If the maternal pancreas cannot raise insulin output enough to overcome this resistance, gestational diabetes develops, usually in the second half of pregnancy.
notes.why: The beta subunit of hCG is close enough to that of LH to activate the LH receptor, so hCG rescues the corpus luteum until placental progesterone output takes over. The placenta is an incomplete steroid factory: it makes progesterone from maternal cholesterol but lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it needs androgen precursors from the fetus. Fetal adrenal DHEA-S, 16-hydroxylated in the fetal liver, is converted by placental sulfatase and aromatase into estriol, which makes maternal estriol a marker of the fetal-placental unit. hPL and other placental hormones blunt maternal insulin signaling, shifting maternal fuel use toward fat so glucose and amino acids are left for the fetus.

points: Plasma volume rises about 40 to 50 percent and red cell mass only about 20 to 30 percent, giving a dilutional anemia.
Cardiac output rises about 30 to 50 percent while systemic vascular resistance falls, so blood pressure dips in the second trimester.
Renal plasma flow and GFR rise about 50 percent, so serum creatinine and BUN fall.
Progesterone drives the respiratory center, raising minute ventilation; PaCO2 falls to about 30 mm Hg (nonpregnant 35 to 45) with a compensated respiratory alkalosis.
Clotting factors and fibrinogen rise and protein S falls; with venous stasis from the uterus this makes pregnancy hypercoagulable.
notes.why: Placental hormones drive most of these changes. Estrogen raises angiotensinogen and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so sodium and water retention expands plasma volume more than erythropoietin expands red cell mass; this dilutes hemoglobin but raises cardiac output and renal plasma flow, so GFR rises and creatinine falls. Vasodilators including progesterone and nitric oxide lower systemic vascular resistance, and progesterone also makes the respiratory center more sensitive to CO2, so ventilation rises, PaCO2 falls, and the kidney excretes bicarbonate to compensate. Higher clotting factors protect against bleeding at delivery but add to the risk of venous thrombosis.

points: In pregnancy estrogen grows the ducts and progesterone grows the alveoli, while prolactin, hPL, cortisol, and insulin ready the alveolar cells.
High placental progesterone blocks milk secretion until delivery; its fall after the placenta is delivered starts copious milk in about 2 to 3 days.
Suckling lowers hypothalamic dopamine, so prolactin rises and drives milk synthesis.
Suckling also releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts myoepithelial cells to eject milk (let-down) and contracts the uterus.
Suckling suppresses GnRH pulses, lowering LH and FSH and delaying ovulation (lactational amenorrhea).
notes.why: Prolactin rises throughout pregnancy, yet copious milk does not flow because high placental progesterone blocks the full secretory response of the alveolar cells. Delivery of the placenta removes this block abruptly, so prolactin can drive full milk synthesis within a few days. Prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone under tonic inhibition, by hypothalamic dopamine, so suckling raises it by lowering dopamine; the same nerve signal also reaches the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei to release oxytocin for milk ejection. Suckling and high prolactin suppress GnRH pulses, which lowers LH and FSH and delays ovulation.

points: Late in pregnancy estrogen adds oxytocin receptors and gap junctions to the myometrium.
The fetal head stretches the cervix, signaling the hypothalamus to release more oxytocin (Ferguson reflex).
Oxytocin and prostaglandins raise myometrial calcium and contraction, which pushes the head harder on the cervix: positive feedback until delivery.
Prostaglandins also soften (ripen) the cervix; prostaglandin inhibitors can delay labor.
notes.why: Labor is a positive feedback loop in which each contraction strengthens the next. Late in pregnancy the myometrium becomes less responsive to progesterone and more responsive to estrogen, which adds oxytocin receptors and gap junctions (connexin 43) so the muscle contracts as one coordinated unit. Cervical stretch sends afferent signals to the hypothalamus, more oxytocin is released, and oxytocin acts through a Gq receptor to raise intracellular calcium and to stimulate prostaglandin synthesis in the decidua. The loop stops only when delivery ends the cervical stretch.

flows.title: Ovarian and endometrial cycle
steps: FSH recruits follicles; the dominant follicle secretes rising estradiol
Estradiol builds proliferative endometrium and lowers FSH
Sustained high estradiol switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge
Ovulation follows about 36 hours after the surge begins
Corpus luteum progesterone turns the endometrium secretory
Without hCG the corpus luteum regresses after about 14 days
Progesterone falls, spiral arteries constrict, and the functional layer sheds

flows.title: Lactation after delivery
steps: Delivery of the placenta drops progesterone
Prolactin now drives copious milk synthesis within about 2 to 3 days
Suckling lowers hypothalamic dopamine, keeping prolactin high
Suckling releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells, ejecting milk
Suckling suppresses GnRH pulses, lowering LH and FSH and delaying ovulation

flows.title: Positive feedback of labor
steps: Fetal head presses on and stretches the cervix
Afferent signals reach the hypothalamus (Ferguson reflex)
Posterior pituitary releases more oxytocin
Oxytocin and prostaglandins raise myometrial calcium; contractions strengthen
Stronger contractions push the head harder against the cervix
The loop repeats until delivery ends the stretch

tricks.label: Count back 14
tricks.text: To find ovulation, count back 14 days from the next period. A 35-day cycle ovulates near day 21; a 28-day cycle near day 14.

tricks.label: Prolactin makes, oxytocin moves
tricks.text: Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin moves it out by squeezing the myoepithelial cells.

tricks.label: Five up, four down
tricks.text: Volume, cardiac output, GFR, ventilation, and clotting go up; vascular resistance, creatinine, PaCO2, and hemoglobin concentration go down.

highYield: A secretory endometrium proves ovulation occurred; anovulatory cycles stay proliferative.
hCG shares its alpha subunit with LH, FSH, and TSH and acts on the LH receptor.
Low maternal estriol can reflect fetal adrenal failure (as in anencephaly) or placental sulfatase deficiency.
A serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL can be abnormal in pregnancy because GFR normally rises.
Gestational diabetes causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia, since glucose crosses the placenta and insulin does not.
Failure to lactate after a postpartum hemorrhage suggests pituitary infarction (Sheehan syndrome).
PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates can cause dangerous hypotension because both raise cGMP.
pitfalls: The follicular phase varies in length; the luteal phase does not.
Prolactin is high throughout pregnancy, yet milk is not made until progesterone falls after delivery.
Pregnancy causes respiratory alkalosis; a normal PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg in late pregnancy suggests CO2 retention.
The anemia of pregnancy is dilutional; red cell mass actually rises.

dumps.p: Draw a 28-day cycle with four stacked panels: pituitary hormones (FSH, LH), ovarian hormones (estradiol, progesterone), the ovary, and the endometrium. Mark ovulation and the length of each phase.
l: FSH rises early to recruit follicles
Estradiol peaks just before the LH surge
LH surge triggers ovulation about day 14
Progesterone peaks in the mid-luteal phase from the corpus luteum
Proliferative endometrium under estrogen; secretory under progesterone
Basal body temperature rises after ovulation
Luteal phase fixed at about 14 days
Falling progesterone causes menses

l: Dilutional anemia from plasma volume outpacing red cell mass
Higher cardiac output with lower systemic vascular resistance
Higher GFR with lower creatinine
Respiratory alkalosis from progesterone-driven ventilation
Hypercoagulable state

Suckling lowers dopamine, raising prolactin for milk synthesis
Suckling releases oxytocin for milk ejection and suppresses GnRH
Cervical stretch raises oxytocin, which strengthens contractions in a positive loop
